edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page, with the id in place of the bare page number at the right margin.

Say 'Use the regular-size blocks, not the big ones', or delete the sentence and have the adult hand out only regular blocks. Read aloud to a K-1 child, 'small blocks' sounds like 'green triangles' and seems to rule out the yellow hexagon that Problem 4 allows.

edits.quote: On each board, circle 1 if the first player can always win, or 2 if the second player can.
edits.fix: Reword for read-aloud, e.g. 'On each board, who can always win? Circle 1 for the player who goes first, 2 for the player who goes second.' The game is correct (answers 1, 2, 1, 1, 2), but 'can always win' needs a plainer form for kindergartners.

edits.quote: Diagram: exactly six outlines of the 16-triangle hexagon, which has exactly six blue coverings (Problem 3 likewise prints exactly 2 + 3 outlines for 2 and 3 coverings)
edits.fix: Add one or two spare outlines here (and in Problem 3) so the number of printed shapes does not give away how many ways exist; the adult can confirm the count at the end.

k-1.summary: A strong, well-stocked K-1 band: six concrete problems on actual-size boards (possible/impossible shapes including an even-area trapezoid that fails, fewest-green triangles, finding all coverings, fewest blocks, a blocking game). All boards and expected answers check out (P4 answers 3, 3, 4; game 1, 2, 1, 1, 2; P6 has exactly 6 coverings). Only small fixes are needed: the footer, the ambiguous 'small blocks' rule, the game wording, and the outline counts that give away 'find all' answers.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.
Say 'Use the regular-size blocks, not the 2x or 3x ones' (or drop it and control the materials), so children do not read it as 'use only green triangles'.

grades-2-3.summary: Kernel 1 is developed through a well-chosen sequence: odd vs even-but-unbalanced boards, boards with holes (two up holes fail, the hourglass fails, one up plus one down works), fewest-green triangles of sides 2-5 with a proof, generalizing to 10 and 100, chevrons that never beat blues (4,5,4,5 vs 2,3,4,5), inventing a 20-triangle board needing 6 greens, and the two-green rule on the hexagon (all 144 up/down placements work). Every diagram is correct and at actual size, the text is lean, and only the footer and the 'small blocks' wording need attention.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.
Say 'Use the regular-size blocks, not the 2x or 3x ones', or drop it and control the materials.

edits.quote: On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges.
edits.fix: Write 'On the hexagon board from Problem 3'. The Problem 1 board, which the previous sentence just mentioned, is also a hexagon (with one ribbon).

edits.quote: Then find the smallest number of flips that changes covering E into covering F in Problem 3, and explain why nobody can do it with fewer.
edits.fix: Problem 3 already asks for this number (it is 8). Rewrite as 'Then explain why nobody can change covering E into covering F (Problem 3) with fewer flips than you found.'

edits.quote: Diagram: a full page of 15 ruled lines with no drawing space
edits.fix: Replace about half the lines with blank space or two small hexagon outlines, so children can sketch ribbons and flips while they build the parity and E-to-F arguments.

grades-4-5.summary: Kernel 2 is developed in depth: all 6 coverings of the (1,2,2) hexagon and their flip graph (diameter 4); decoded A-B, C-D and E-F flip distances of 3, 4 and 8; a 4-flip loop from A that exists because A has disjoint flippable hexagons; ribbons with a correct LRRLR example; the parity proof; and counts of 20 for both the (2,2,2) and (1,3,3) hexagons. There is more than forty minutes of work, all of it correct. Only small fixes are needed: an ambiguous 'hexagon board' reference, a question that repeats Problem 3, the footer, and a proof page with no room to draw.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 band builds the coloring argument through well-chosen contrasting boards (unbalanced even-area boards, holes, the hourglass, chevrons, inventing a board, the two-green rule), with every diagram correct and at actual size.
overall.weakest: The K-1 band has a few small read-aloud issues: the 'small blocks' rule conflicts with the hexagon allowed in Problem 4, the 'can always win' wording needs simplifying, and the 'find all' pages print exactly as many outlines as there are answers, which gives the counts away.
